title: 157 Enteric methane emissions of beef cattle grazing on native sagebrush in Eastern Oregon
content:
Abstract
Methane (CH₄) production in cattle is a significant aspect of agricultural greenhouse gas emissions, contributing to climate change. Ruminants, produce CH₄ primarily through a process called enteric fermentation. Cattle break down cellulose and other complex carbohydrates, and methanogenic microbes in the rumen convert hydrogen and carbon dioxide into CH₄, which is then expelled through belching. The goal of this study was to quantify CH₄ emissions from cattle raised in the Western U.S., where cows are typically fed during the winter and graze on native rangelands from spring to fall. A total of twenty-two cows (Angus × Hereford) were randomly selected from the Eastern Oregon Agricultural Research Center (EOARC) herd, and were acclimated in the spring to Greenfeed Pasture System monitoring units (C-Lock) to measure CH₄ emissions (g/day). During this acclimation period, the cows were maintained as a group and provided meadow hay ad libitum, which contained 8.5% CP and 56% TDN. Once the cows were acclimated to the monitoring systems, they, along with the monitoring units, were moved to the Northern Great Basin Experimental Range (NGBER) in Riley, OR, to assess CH₄ emissions during the grazing season. The monitoring units were strategically placed near water sources and programmed to record up to 8 visits per cow each day, with alfalfa pellets used as an enticement. Throughout the study, cow body weight (BW) and body condition scores (BCS) were recorded. Additionally, the cows’ locations and grazing behavior were tracked using virtual fence collars (Vence, Merck). Preliminary data for CH4 emissions for the spring season (5 weeks), were analyzed over time as repeated measures, including week, and period of the day (morning, afternoon, evening, and night) using cow as a covariate (P < 0.001), using the MIXED procedure of SAS (SAS Inst. Inc., Cary, NC, USA). Statistical significance was defined at P ≤ 0.05. There were effects of week (P = 0.03) and period (P < 0.0001) for CH₄ emissions. Methane emissions gradually increased over time peaking on week 5 (180 vs. 210 g/cow daily, respectively for week 1 and 5). For the period of the day CH4 emissions were the lowest in the morning (6:00 to 11:59 am; 143 g/cow), intermediate in the afternoon (12:00 to 5:59 pm; 193 g/cow), and greatest in the evening (6:00 to 11:59 pm; 221 g/cow) and night (12:00 to 5:59 am; 218 g/cow), with no effects between evening and night (P = 0.77). Additionally, from spring to summer, cow BW changed (P = 0.001) approximately 13kg (545 vs. 558 kg, respectively, for spring and summer). These preliminary data present a large variation in CH4 emissions over time and also within the day, which should be accounted for when evaluating CH4 emissions of cattle.
